title: From dashboard questions to panel data

blocks.content: Explore two dashboards on Grafana Play. They use sample data, not measurements from a real service. You don't need an account and won't change or save anything.
You'll see how panels answer questions about changes over time and values on a scale.
Open **Grafana Dashboard**. This demo uses sample data to show different panel types. The tour explains what each panel displays.

The **Memory / CPU** panel uses a line chart to answer the question "How is resource use changing over time?" Time runs along the horizontal axis. In this demo, the line shows generated values, not separate CPU and memory measurements.
blocks.tooltip: Read changes from left to right along the time axis.

blocks.content: The **logins** panel uses a line chart to answer the question "How does the number of logins change over time?" The rises and falls show changes across the selected period.
blocks.tooltip: Rises and falls make changes over time visible.

blocks.content: The **server requests** panel uses a line chart to answer the question "How does request volume change over time?" Each line shows a server's values across the selected period, so you can compare their changes.
blocks.tooltip: Separate lines let you compare changes across servers.

blocks.content: The **Google hits** panel uses percentage bar gauges to answer the question "Where does each value fall between 0 and 100%?" Each bar shows one series' average over the selected period.
blocks.tooltip: Bar length shows an average's position on the percentage scale.

blocks.content: The **Google hits** panel shown here uses horizontal bar gauges to answer the question "How do these values compare?" Each bar has a label and a number. The shared scale makes larger and smaller values easy to compare.
blocks.tooltip: Compare bar lengths and read the numbers beside their labels.

blocks.content: The **Google hits** panel shown here uses a gauge to answer the question "Where does this value fall on its scale?" The filled arc shows one value's position between the scale's minimum and maximum. It doesn't show a trend over time.
blocks.tooltip: The filled arc shows one value's position on the scale.

blocks.content: The **Google hits** panel shown here uses named bar gauges to answer the question "How do the values compare across servers?" Each server has its own bar. Unlike a line chart, these bars show averages, not changes over time.
blocks.tooltip: Each named bar shows one server's average.

blocks.content: You've seen how line charts show changes over time, while gauges and bar gauges show values on a scale.
You'll see which value a gauge displays and how its unit and scale help you read it.

The **Memory** panel uses a gauge to answer the question "How much memory is in use on average, and how close is it to the displayed maximum?" Its value is the mean, or average, over the selected period, not the latest sample.
blocks.tooltip: The displayed number is an average over the selected period.

blocks.content: The **Memory** panel displays its value in bytes, marked with a suffix such as B. Its scale runs from 0 to 300 bytes. These settings show how to read the sample value; they aren't a real server's memory capacity.
blocks.tooltip: Read the number with its unit and the scale's limits.

blocks.content: You've seen how the average, byte unit, and scale determine what the gauge shows.
You'll see which data source and query supply a bar chart's values.
Open the **Popular JS Frameworks** panel in the editor to view its query and chart. Leave the settings unchanged.
The **Popular JS Frameworks** panel gets its data from TestData, a source of sample data. The query tells TestData which sample to return.
blocks.tooltip: The selected data source supplies the query's results.

blocks.content: The **Popular JS Frameworks** panel uses the **CSV File** scenario to read `js_libraries.csv`. These settings form its query. Some data sources use query controls like these; others use text such as SQL or PromQL.
blocks.tooltip: Query controls depend on the selected data source.

blocks.content: You've seen how the query tells TestData to return rows from a sample CSV file.

blocks.title: From returned rows to a chart

blocks.content: You'll see the query results as rows, then find the same values in the chart.
The **Popular JS Frameworks** panel can show its query results as rows. Turn on **Table view** to view them. This changes only the preview, not the query or saved dashboard.
blocks.tooltip: View the query results as rows instead of bars.

blocks.hint: Turn on Table view in the panel editor to show the returned rows.
blocks.content: The **Popular JS Frameworks** panel receives four columns: **Library**, **Github Stars**, **Forks**, and **Watchers**. Each row names a library and gives its counts. These fixed sample figures aren't current counts from GitHub.
blocks.tooltip: Each row pairs a library name with three numeric values.

blocks.hint: Keep Table view on to view the React.js row.
blocks.content: The **Popular JS Frameworks** panel receives 169000 stars, 34000 forks, and 6700 watchers for React.js. The chart uses the library name as a category and draws a bar for each count.
blocks.tooltip: One category can have several numeric values.

blocks.content: Return to the **Popular JS Frameworks** panel's chart without saving any editor changes.

The **Popular JS Frameworks** panel answers the question "How do the counts compare across libraries?" React.js's star-count bar shows the same 169000 you saw in its row. The bars display the query results; they don't change the values.
blocks.tooltip: The bars show the same values as the query-result rows.

blocks.content: You've seen how query-result rows become bars and how a panel's calculation and unit help you read its values.
Continue to Choosing a visualization to see which panel types answer different questions.
